scenes.title: Separate model and tool
scenes.body: A maker, a distribution platform, and a client play different roles.
scenes.narration: When the dropdown says Claude, you might ask who makes the model, where it runs, and which tool you're using. Those are three questions. The maker publishes the model, a provider or platform offers access, and the client gives you a workflow. In this lesson, the catalogs are a dated snapshot. Your approved picker tells you what is available for work.
scenes.code:
Maker → model family and version
Platform → deployment or service
Client → model picker and workflow
scenes.result: Example: a Claude model can appear in Copilot.
scenes.focus: Maker, distribution platform and client are separate entries
scenes.action: Label the three layers for an installed model.

scenes.title: Read the OpenAI catalog
scenes.body: Use vendor categories to identify candidate models.
scenes.narration: Open the OpenAI model catalog and compare the entries for GPT six point two Sol and Astra. In the snapshot, Sol is positioned for everyday coding and agent work. Astra is positioned for more demanding reasoning and coding. Notice the input and output section on each card. If you need transcription or image generation, read the relevant entry instead of inferring it from the name.

scenes.title: Read the Claude catalog
scenes.narration: In Anthropic’s catalog, find Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, and Fable. Their cards describe different speed, workload, and capability tradeoffs. The provider table matters when you use Claude Code remotely. Two environments can show the same family name while resolving a shortcut differently. Record the exact model ID or selector label you can verify in the approved session.
scenes.code:
Haiku 5.5 → lower latency and cost
Sonnet 5.5 → balanced everyday work
Opus 5.5 → complex tasks
Fable 5.2 → demanding, long agent work

scenes.title: Read Microsoft and Foundry
scenes.body: Foundry lists models from Microsoft and other makers.
scenes.narration: In Microsoft Foundry, inspect the publisher on a model card. The catalog includes models published by Microsoft as well as models from other providers. You may see Microsoft’s MAI or Phi families. MAI Code two Flash was a limited-access preview in the snapshot. Check the actual card and deployment conditions before you put a catalog model on your team's available list.

scenes.title: Read availability and status
scenes.body: Use the dated catalog and the approved picker together.
scenes.narration: Pick a model card and compare its release status with the workplace picker. Preview on the card describes the provider’s offering. Your company’s policy, plan, and configured provider determine whether you can select it. Put both observations in your note. A colleague can then tell the difference between a catalog announcement and an option they can use today.

scenes.title: Make a dated record
scenes.body: Keep a short record so model examples can be refreshed.
scenes.narration: Make one inventory entry for the class. Include the maker, the exact version or label, the client and environment, and the date you checked. If the picker changes later, repeat that short check. With the available options in hand, the next lesson will compare models on a bug whose behavior you can verify yourself.
